fields.claim_quote: Since there aren't any edge the number of vertices must be equal to $1$ or $0$.
fields.explanation: Zero edges place no upper bound of one on the vertex count: two isolated vertices give an edgeless graph with two vertices. The selected Lean statement uses the actual empty SimpleGraph on Fin2 and proves zero edges and failure of card<=1. It does not certify the separate proposed construction step, empirical counts or runtime.
fields.flaw: The quoted base-case assertion says that any graph with zero edges has 0 or 1 vertices. The edgeless graph on two vertices refutes this assertion.
fields.problem: Is my induction proof of the handshake lemma correct? (Graph Theory)
fields.source_context:
0001 | I am an high-school senior who loves maths, I decided to taught myself some basic Graph Theory and I tried to prove the handshake lemma using induction.
0002 | 
0003 | While unable to find any proofs similar to the one I wrote on the Internet, I wonder if mine is incorrect or just presented differently. Any advice, remarks or critic would be warmly welcomed!
0004 | 
0005 | Let P be the following proposition "In any graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is equal to twice the number of edges:"
0006 | 
0007 | $$\textrm{P(n)}:\sum_{V\;\in\;G} deg(|V|) = 2n\;\;\;where\;\;|E| = n\\$$
0008 | 
0009 | Base case:  $P(0): 2n = 0 |_{n=0}.$ Since there aren't any edge the number of vertices must be equal to $1$ or $0$.
0010 | 
0011 | $$\sum_{V\;\in\;G} deg(|V|) = deg(|V|) = 0\;\text{the number degree equal to }0.\\\text{thus, }P(0)\text{ is true}$$
0012 | 
0013 | Induction step: Assuming that $P(n)$ is true for a given natural number.Let show that $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1).$
0014 | 
0015 | 
0016 | $$P(n):\sum_{V\;\in\;G} deg(|V|) = 2n\\
0017 | \sum_{V\;\in\;G} deg(|V|) + 2= 2n + 2\\
0018 | \sum_{V\;\in\;G} deg(|V|) + 2 = 2(n+1)\\
0019 | which\;yield\;by\;adding\;two\;vertices\;of\;degree\;1\\P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$$
0020 | 
0021 | $$\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \sum_{V\;\in\;G} deg(|V|) = 2|E|\\
fields.witness: Take the graph V={0,1}, E=empty. It has zero edges and two vertices, contradicting the quoted base-case assertion that the number of vertices must be 0 or 1. Both degrees are zero, so the handshake identity itself still holds. This is the selected Lean counterexample.

scope_metadata.target_scope: The quoted assertion that an edgeless graph has at most one vertex; not the handshake lemma or an exhaustive characterization of the induction construction.
